fact_pattern: An Employee spends a Travel Day in a Tier 3 city. The travel is not Client-Billable Travel. No Pre-Approval of any kind has been obtained. The Employee is not engaged on Critical Incident Response. The Employee incurs GBP 500 of meal expense on the day. The record of meals provided at no cost carries the value -10 (a corrupt or mis-signed free-meal count; no meal was in fact provided free). The Policy caps this day at GBP 40 and contains no provision capable of raising that figure on these facts, yet the module reimburses GBP 190.
source_reasoning: E-3.1(c) fixes the Tier 3 entitlement at reimbursement of meal expenses 'up to' GBP 40 per Travel Day. Every clause capable of displacing or raising that figure is inapplicable on these facts: E-3.2 requires Client-Billable Travel (false); E-3.3 requires Pre-Approval for a specified higher amount (none obtained, and no amount specified); E-7.2 requires Critical Incident Response (false). E-3.4 is the only other clause that touches the day's per diem, and it is reduction-only in terms - 'the per diem for that Travel Day IS REDUCED by GBP 15 in respect of each such meal' - and its operative fact is a meal 'provided at no cost to the Employee', of which there can only be nought or more. No reading of E-3.4 permits it to increase the per diem, so nothing in the Policy can carry this day above GBP 40. The module nevertheless computes e3_4_reduction = 15 * (-10) = -150 and then adjusted_per_diem = max(0, 40 - (-150)) = 190, paying GBP 190 - GBP 150 more than the ceiling E-3.1(c) imposes. The defect is an unguarded input domain on meals_provided_free: the declaration is a bare 'integer' with no lower bound and no assertion, and the sign of the reduction is never checked. The sibling module claimwindow does guard its analogous ordering assumption ('assertion submission_date >= expense_incurred_date'), which shows the guard was available and was simply omitted here. The correct behaviour is either to reject the input as it does not describe any state of affairs the Policy recognises, or to treat the free-meal count as nought or more so that E-3.4 applies no reduction and E-3.1(c) governs, giving GBP 40. On either correct behaviour the module's GBP 190 is wrong, and it errs in the direction of over-payment, silently, with no error raised. Magnitude scales without bound with the magnitude of the corrupt count.
attacks_tried: free-meal count -1 on Tier 1: observed adjusted_per_diem 90.00 against an E-3.1(a) cap of 75.00, confirming the same defect at the other tier
free-meal counts 0,1,2,3,4 on Tier 3: 40/25/10/0/0, correct and correctly floored at nought by Money.max

same unguarded-domain attack on groundtransport TaxiFare: journey_start_hour 10 with journey_start_minute 5000 yields minutes_after_midnight 5600, satisfying the E-5.3 airport carve-out and reimbursing 100.00 without limit; and journey_start_hour -1 likewise. Not recorded as a separate BREAK because no clean prose fact pattern states a journey time in that form

same attack on accommodation NightlyAccommodation: parking_cost -100 with Tier 1 room 400 yields reimbursable_amount 120.00, i.e. below the E-4.1 cap the module itself computed. Not recorded separately for the same reason
negative meal_expense_incurred
sub-penny meal_expense_incurred 0.01: reimbursable 0.01, correct

fact_pattern: An Employee spends a Travel Day in a Tier 1 city on travel that is not Client-Billable. Two meals are provided at no cost as part of a conference. The Employee incurs GBP 20 of meal expense out of pocket on the day. No Pre-Approval; no Critical Incident Response.
expected: Not determinable from the document. Reading (1), the per diem is a CEILING and E-3.4 reduces the ceiling: ceiling 75 - 30 = 45, reimbursement = min(20, 45) = GBP 20. Reading (2), the per diem is the AMOUNT PAYABLE and E-3.4 reduces that amount: payable = min(20, 75) = 20, then 20 - 30 = -10, floored at GBP 0.
source_reasoning: The Policy never states the order in which E-3.4's GBP 15 per-meal reduction and E-3.1's 'up to' limit against actual spend are applied, and the two orders do not commute whenever the free-meal reduction exceeds the headroom between actual spend and the tier figure. The document supplies textual support for each order and settles neither. Reading (1) is supported by E-3.1, which states its figures as amounts the Employee may be reimbursed 'up to', i.e. ceilings, so that E-3.4's reduction of 'the per diem' naturally reduces the ceiling; on those words the module's GBP 20 is right. Reading (2) is supported by E-3.5, which uses the same defined phrase in the opposite sense - 'No PER DIEM IS PAYABLE in respect of a Travel Day on which the Employee does not incur any meal expense' - treating the per diem as the sum paid rather than a ceiling; if 'per diem' in E-3.4 bears the meaning E-3.5 gives it one clause later, E-3.4 reduces the payment and the answer is GBP 0. E-3.4 and E-3.5 are in the same section, adopted at the same time, and use the same term inconsistently. The module commits to reading (1) without the document compelling it, and the choice is worth GBP 20 on these facts. A drafting fix in the Policy, not the code, is what is needed: E-3.4 should say whether it reduces the applicable per diem figure or the amount otherwise payable.
attacks_tried: Tier 3 with 3 and 4 free meals to drive the figure negative: 0 and 0, floored, which is correct since no clause authorises a negative reimbursement or a clawback

free meals combined with an E-3.3 Pre-Approved cap of 300 and spend 250: adjusted 255, reimbursed 250 - the reduction is applied to whichever clause supplied the cap, which E-3.4's words ('the per diem for that Travel Day') require

free meals combined with the E-3.2 1.5x multiplier to test whether the reduction is applied before or after the multiplier - the module multiplies first, which E-3.4 requires since it operates on 'the per diem for that Travel Day', i.e. the E-3.2 figure

fact_pattern: An Employee spends a Travel Day in a Tier 1 city on Client-Billable Travel. The statement of work specifies no per diem figure, so the E-3.2 fallback gives 1.5 x GBP 75 = GBP 112.50. Before the trip the Employee obtained written Pre-Approval from a person with GBP 500 of delegated authority for a specified per diem of GBP 100. Actual meal spend on the day is GBP 300.
expected: Not determinable from the document. Reading (1), 'higher' is measured against the per diem that would otherwise apply, here the E-3.2 figure of 112.50: GBP 100 is not higher, E-3.3 is not engaged, and GBP 112.50 applies. Reading (2), 'higher' is measured against the E-3.1 table figure of 75: GBP 100 is higher, E-3.3 is engaged as an exception to E-3.2 as well, and GBP 100 applies.
source_reasoning: E-3.3 reads 'By way of exception to E-3.1 and E-3.2, where Pre-Approval has been obtained for A SPECIFIED HIGHER AMOUNT, that amount applies.' The comparator for 'higher' is left unstated, and the two candidates diverge precisely where E-3.2 has already lifted the per diem above the E-3.1 table. Reading (2) has the literal support that E-3.1 is where the amounts are actually tabulated, so 'higher' most obviously means higher than the table; but it produces the perverse result that a Pre-Approval obtained for the Employee's benefit REDUCES the per diem from 112.50 to 100, which the word 'higher' and the character of E-3.3 as a relieving exception both resist. Reading (1), which the module adopts via its internal per_diem_apart_from_e3_3, gives 'exception to ... E-3.2' real content by measuring against whichever of E-3.1 and E-3.2 is in fact applicable, and makes E-3.3 monotone. It is the better reading, but the document does not compel it, and the choice is worth GBP 12.50 a day. The Policy should state the comparator. A related unresolved case: where the Pre-Approved amount is lower than the tier figure itself (Tier 1, non-Client-Billable, specified 50), the module returns 75 rather than 50, on the same reading - E-3.3 simply is not engaged.
attacks_tried: Pre-Approved 200 against a Client-Billable 112.50: 200, so E-3.3 does defeat E-3.2 when the amount is genuinely higher - the exception chain e3_3 -> e3_2 -> e3_1_cap resolves correctly
Pre-Approved 100 non-Client-Billable against 75: 100, so E-3.3 also defeats E-3.1 directly even though its Catala parent e3_2 is inapplicable - no Conflict and no NoValue
Pre-Approved 50 non-Client-Billable against 75: 75
Pre-Approved 75 exactly equal to the tier figure: 75, the strict > gate makes no difference at equality
Client-Billable with a statement-of-work figure of 30 below the tier figure and Pre-Approval for 60: 60, E-3.3 correctly measured against the applicable 30
Pre-Approval with approver authority 100 against a specified 200: rejected, cap falls back to 75, correct under E-2.4

fact_pattern: An Employee is engaged on Critical Incident Response within the meaning of Annex C paragraph C-2.5 (a Severity 1 incident, between declaration and formal closure) and spends a Travel Day in a Tier 1 city. The travel is Client-Billable Travel and the executed statement of work specifies a per diem of GBP 100. Actual meal spend GBP 300. No Pre-Approval.
expected: Not determinable from the document. Reading (A), E-7.2 amends the named quantity 'the per diem under E-3.1' to 95; E-3.2's specified-amount limb never refers to that quantity, so the uplift has no effect and GBP 100 applies. Reading (B), E-7.2 is a flat uplift to whatever per diem is applicable, giving 100 + 20 = GBP 120.
source_reasoning: E-7.2 says 'the per diem under E-3.1 is increased by GBP 20 per Travel Day and Pre-Approval is not required for that increase.' On Client-Billable Travel with a statement-of-work figure, the applicable per diem is supplied wholly by E-3.2's first limb and is not 'under E-3.1' at all, so on reading (A) the clause E-7.2 fires but is entirely vacuous: the module does compute per_diem_under_e3_1 = 95 and then discards it, and the Employee on a Severity 1 incident receives exactly what a colleague on ordinary client work in the same city receives. That is a branch that is live in the code and dead in effect, which is the classic signature of a flattened exception. Reading (B) avoids the vacuity and draws support from E-7.2's closing words: the drafter's express disapplication of Pre-Approval 'for that increase' presupposes an increase that actually reaches the Employee's entitlement, which on reading (A) it does not here. But nothing in either document states which quantity the GBP 20 attaches to where E-3.2 governs, and reading (A) follows the words E-7.2 actually uses, so no clause compels reading (B). The same ambiguity bites, with the opposite sign, where the statement of work specifies a figure BELOW the tier figure (Client-Billable, statement-of-work 30, Critical Incident Response): the module pays 30 for a Severity 1 incident day in a Tier 1 city. E-7.2 should name the quantity it uplifts and say whether it survives E-3.2 and E-3.3.
attacks_tried: Critical Incident Response non-Client-Billable Tier 1: 95, and Tier 3: 60 - the flat GBP 20 is added to the tier figure as E-7.2 requires

Critical Incident Response plus Client-Billable with NO statement-of-work figure: 142.50, i.e. 1.5 x (75+20) under reading (A) rather than 1.5 x 75 + 20 = 132.50 under reading (B) - the same unresolved question, worth GBP 10 there
Critical Incident Response plus Client-Billable with no statement-of-work figure plus Pre-Approval for 120: 142.50, the Pre-Approval correctly not engaged because 120 is not higher than 142.50

fact_pattern: An Employee is engaged on Critical Incident Response within the meaning of Annex C paragraph C-2.5 and spends a Travel Day in a Tier 1 city on travel that is not Client-Billable. Before the trip the Employee obtained written Pre-Approval from a person with GBP 500 of delegated authority for a specified per diem of GBP 120. Actual meal spend GBP 300.
expected: Not determinable from the document. Reading (A), E-3.3 substitutes the Pre-Approved amount for the uplifted E-3.1 figure entirely, giving GBP 120 - the GBP 20 survives only through E-3.3's 'higher amount' test, which measures 120 against 95. Reading (B), the E-7.2 uplift is a separate additive entitlement for which 'Pre-Approval is not required', so it stacks on the Pre-Approved amount: 120 + 20 = GBP 140.
source_reasoning: The document does not say whether the E-7.2 uplift is cumulative with, or substituted by, an E-3.3 Pre-Approved amount. E-3.3 is expressed as an exception to E-3.1 and E-3.2 only - it says nothing about E-7.2 - and E-7.2 is expressed as an amendment to E-3.1 rather than as a free-standing allowance, which supports reading (A) and the module's GBP 120. Against that, E-7.2's closing words 'and Pre-Approval is not required for that increase' single the increase out as something Pre-Approval has no purchase on, which reads naturally as making the GBP 20 immune to the Pre-Approval machinery altogether rather than merely unnecessary to it; on reading (A) an Employee who obtains a Pre-Approval is worse off than the arithmetic sum of the two reliefs, and the GBP 20 is silently absorbed. Neither clause contains a 'notwithstanding', an 'in addition to' or an 'in substitution for' to resolve it, so there is no compulsion either way. The choice is worth GBP 20 a day. Note the interaction is also non-monotone in a way the drafter is unlikely to have intended: at a Pre-Approved 90 the module returns 95 (E-3.3 not engaged, uplift intact), at 120 it returns 120 (E-3.3 engaged, uplift absorbed), so the marginal value of raising a Pre-Approval from 90 to 120 is GBP 25 rather than GBP 30.
attacks_tried: Critical Incident Response plus Pre-Approval for 90, below the uplifted 95: 95, the uplift survives because E-3.3's higher-amount gate is measured against the uplifted figure

Critical Incident Response plus Client-Billable with no statement-of-work figure plus Pre-Approval 300 plus 3 free meals, spend 250: cap 300, adjusted 255, reimbursed 250 - the full stack resolves without Conflict or NoValue
Pre-Approval obtained on the day the expense was incurred: rejected, cap falls back to 75 - see the separate E-2.4 finding

fact_pattern: On the morning of 10 June 2025 an Employee obtains written approval from a person holding GBP 500 of delegated financial authority for an expense of GBP 200. The Employee incurs the GBP 200 expense that same afternoon, after the approval was given. The Policy's definition of Pre-Approval is satisfied on those facts, but the module's input model records only calendar dates, so the approval and the expense are indistinguishable in time and the module resolves the tie against the Employee.
expected: Not determinable on these inputs, and that is the finding. On the stated facts E-2.4 is satisfied and valid = true. On the mirror-image facts the same inputs equally describe - approval given at 16:00 for an expense incurred at 09:00 - E-2.4 is not satisfied and valid = false. The input model cannot separate them, so the module must either carry a timestamp or declare the case indeterminate rather than silently answer false.
source_reasoning: E-2.4 defines Pre-Approval as 'written approval obtained BEFORE THE EXPENSE IS INCURRED from a person holding delegated financial authority at or above the threshold of the expense.' The operative comparison is between two moments in time, not two calendar days. The module encodes it as 'obtained_at < expense_incurred_at' over date-granular inputs, so every same-day Pre-Approval - the ordinary case for a taxi booked in the morning or a fare approved hours before travel - is treated as too late, and a whole class of approvals that E-2.4 plainly validates is unreachable through the input schema. The strict comparison is the safer of the two available resolutions, since the permissive one (<=) would validate approvals actually obtained after the spend, contrary to E-2.4. But the honest answer on these inputs is that neither is right: the ambiguity is in the model, and it is the corpus that fails to define a timestamp for either the approval or the expense. The consequence is not confined to this scope - mealperdiem routes E-3.3 through PreApprovalValid, so a same-day Pre-Approval for a Tier 1 specified amount of 200 yields a per_diem_cap of 75 instead of 200 (a GBP 125 swing, reproduced), and groundtransport routes E-5.2 through it, so a first class ticket approved the same morning is reimbursed at nil.
attacks_tried: approval dated the day before: valid true
approver authority exactly equal to the expense amount: valid true, correct for E-2.4's 'at or above'
approver authority one penny short: valid false, correct
approval not in writing: rejected, correct for E-2.4's 'written approval'
approval flagged obtained false: rejected
downstream effect confirmed in mealperdiem (cap 75 not 200) and considered for groundtransport E-5.2

fact_pattern: An Employee stays one night in a Tier 3 city. The hotel bill is GBP 200 for the room, GBP 15 of local taxes and a GBP 10 mandatory city charge, plus GBP 25 of parking. No evidence is provided that no compliant accommodation was available within the cap.
expected: Not determinable from the document. Narrow reading: E-4.1 is the only clause in E-4 that confers reimbursement and it confers it on 'accommodation' up to GBP 120 in a Tier 3 city; parking is not accommodation and no clause reimburses it, so the E-4 answer is GBP 120 and parking falls to be dealt with under E-1.2. Wide reading: E-4.3's express exclusion of parking from the cap implies parking is reimbursable outside the cap, giving GBP 120 + GBP 25 = GBP 145.
source_reasoning: E-4.3 says only what the caps in E-4.1 measure: they are 'inclusive of local taxes and of any mandatory resort or city charge, and EXCLUSIVE OF THE COST OF PARKING.' It confers no entitlement. E-4.1 is the sole conferring provision in E-4 and its subject is accommodation, capped per night. The module's headline output reimburses parking in full and without any limit, so the total paid for a Tier 3 night (GBP 145) exceeds the only cap the Policy states for that night (GBP 120), on the strength of an implication rather than a clause. The implication is a fair one and I do not say it is wrong, but the usual argument for it - that otherwise E-4.3's exclusion would do no work - does not hold: the exclusion has a complete and sufficient function on the narrow reading too, namely to stop parking from crowding accommodation out of the cap, so that a GBP 235 bill of which GBP 25 is parking is measured against the cap as GBP 210 rather than GBP 235. Because that justification for the wide reading fails, the reading rests on implication alone and the document does not compel it. A second, separate hazard in the same output: parking is reimbursed with no cap of any kind, so an arbitrarily large parking charge is paid in full; and because it is added after the cap, a negative parking figure reduces the total below the cap the module itself computed (Tier 1, room 400, parking -100 gives reimbursable_amount 120 against an applicable_cap of 220, reproduced). The Policy should say expressly whether parking is reimbursable and, if so, subject to what limit.
attacks_tried: E-4.2 reachability without evidence: the 1.4x uplift is gated solely on the evidence input and cannot be reached with it false - Tier 1 room 400 with no evidence gives 220, with evidence 308. The non-computable predicate is taken as an input and is not inferred from the cost exceeding the cap, so there is no judgement laundering
1.4x arithmetic at each tier: 308 / 224 / 168, exact
cost exactly at the cap (Tier 1, 220): 220 reimbursed in full, correct for 'up to'

E-4.3 inclusivity: Tier 1 room 180 + tax 20 + charge 20 gives cost_against_cap 220 and is reimbursed in full, whereas room 200 + tax 15 + charge 10 gives 225 and is capped at 220 - the taxes and mandatory charge are correctly counted against the cap, so getting E-4.3 wrong would have changed the answer and the module gets it right

fact_pattern: An Employee travels out and back on Company business on 1 May 2025, departing and returning on the same calendar day and not staying away overnight.
expected: Not determinable from the document. Reading (1), the overnight requirement in E-2.3's first sentence is a precondition and the second sentence merely tells you to count both endpoint days of a genuine overnight trip: 0 Travel Days. Reading (2), the second sentence is a deeming provision - 'The day of departure and the day of return ARE EACH a Travel Day' - which by its terms is unqualified and deems the departure and return days to be Travel Days whether or not the Employee is away overnight: 1 Travel Day, the departure and return falling on the same calendar day.
source_reasoning: E-2.3 has two sentences that pull against each other. The first makes being 'away from their principal place of work OVERNIGHT' constitutive of a Travel Day. The second is flatly declarative and carries no overnight qualifier of its own. If the second sentence is read as subordinate to the first, a same-day return produces no Travel Day at all and the module's 0 is right. If it is read as a deeming provision - and the emphatic 'are each' is the language of deeming rather than of explanation - then the departure day is a Travel Day on its own terms and a same-day trip yields 1. The module commits to reading (1) with no tie-breaker in the document, and on a Tier 1 same-day trip the choice is worth GBP 75 of meal per diem under E-3.1(a). I note the module is at least self-consistent: the same reading makes travel_days equal nights + 1, which is right on any overnight trip. The Policy should qualify the second sentence expressly.
attacks_tried: one-night trip, depart 1 May return 2 May: 2, correct on either reading - the day of departure and the day of return are each a Travel Day
two-night trip, depart 1 May return 3 May: 3, correct, nights + 1 with no double count of the return day
return before departure: 0, garbage input handled without error

a red-eye absence of seven hours spanning midnight (depart 1 May, return 2 May) yields 2 Travel Days and GBP 150 in a Tier 1 city - generous, but exactly what E-2.3 read with E-3.1 says, so not a finding

fact_pattern: The E-6.1 / E-6.2 / E-6.3 staircase was probed at and around both boundaries, with and without the line manager's certification, and no fact pattern was found on which the module's answer differs from what E-6 requires. This entry is evidence of coverage, not approval.
source_reasoning: Every boundary matches the clause text. E-6.1 'within 60 days after the date on which the expense was incurred' admits day 60 and excludes day 61, and the module returns admissible at 59 and 60 and inadmissible at 61 absent certification. E-6.2 'after 60 days but within 120 days' covers exactly days 61 to 120 inclusive, and the module's exception fires at 61, 119 and 120 with certification and not at 60 or 121. E-6.3's long-stop 'more than 120 days ... in any circumstances' is inadmissible at 121 and at 500 even with certification, and nothing in the module can defeat it: the only exception below e6_3 is e6_2, whose own condition is bounded at 120, so there is no path to admissibility beyond day 120. Leap-year spans were checked (1 January 2024 to 1 March 2024 is 60 days, admissible) and the day arithmetic is calendar-correct rather than month-approximated. The one thing the module declines to answer is a claim submitted BEFORE the expense was incurred, where 'assertion submission_date >= expense_incurred_date' raises rather than returning a value. That is a defensible refusal rather than a break: E-6 measures every limb forward from the date the expense was incurred and gives no rule for a claim that precedes it, so there is nothing in the document the module could be said to contradict. It does mean the module cannot process a claim for a pre-booked expense submitted ahead of the incurring date, which is a real if narrow operational gap.

fact_pattern: The E-5.3 GBP 60 journey limit and the airport carve-out for journeys before 06:00 or after 22:00 were probed at every boundary minute, and the E-5.2 first class rule was probed across the fare comparison and the Pre-Approval limb. No fact pattern was found on which either scope's answer differs from what E-5 requires. This entry is evidence of coverage, not approval.
source_reasoning: E-5.3's carve-out is for a journey 'before 06:00 or after 22:00', which is strict at both ends: 05:59 is before 06:00, 06:00 is not; 22:01 is after 22:00, 22:00 is not. The module returns the uncapped GBP 100 at 05:59 and 22:01 and the capped GBP 60 at 06:00 and 22:00, which is exactly the text, and it returns GBP 60 at every one of those times when the journey is not an airport journey, so the carve-out is properly conditioned on the airport predicate and not inferred from the hour alone. Midnight and 23:59 airport journeys are uncapped, correctly, both being outside 06:00 to 22:00. A cost of exactly GBP 60 is reimbursed in full, correct for 'up to GBP 60'. On E-5.2, 'reimbursable ONLY WHERE the ticket cost does not exceed the standard class fare ... or where Pre-Approval has been obtained' is a condition of reimbursability, not a cap: a first class ticket that fails both limbs is not reimbursable at all, and nil rather than the standard class fare is the right answer because the Employee did not buy standard class and E-5.1 confers nothing on first class travel. The module returns nil at ticket 200 against a same-day standard fare of 150 and the full 200 where valid Pre-Approval exists, with 'does not exceed' correctly inclusive at ticket 150. Pre-Approval is routed through E-2.4 and correctly fails where the approver's authority (100 or 180) is below the ticket cost, where the approval is oral, and where it is dated the day of travel - that last case being the E-2.4 granularity ambiguity recorded separately, not a defect of this module.
